source.title: Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: A Theoretical Analysis of Multi-Epoch Scaling in Linear Regression
source.authors: Tingkai Yan; Haodong Wen; Binghui Li; Kairong Luo; Wenguang Chen; Kaifeng Lyu

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure text is garbled in the web extraction, but the main text describes the relevant experimental findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines data-reuse scaling claims with theoretical and empirical results, arguing that reuse benefits depend on dataset size and distribution and are not captured by a uniform effective epoch count.
record.gate_note: The study tests data reuse and scaling in linear regression and LLM pretraining. It does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, or downstream task predictability. The LLM validation-loss curves are mostly presented in figures; the text reports derived effective-reuse results and saturation-point fits rather than a fitted held-out-loss power law.
record.test_reason: The LLM experiments (one 0.3B model, 0.2B–2B fresh tokens, up to 100 epochs) test whether repeated-data pretraining matches fresh-data loss. Repeated tokens count as fresh only up to a saturation point that grows with dataset size. The authors argue this means data-constrained scaling laws need restating, so the study bears on V5's repeated-data regime. The linear-regression theory and simulations are a stylised model, not language models, and do not bear on any version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the effective reuse rate E(K,N)≈K for small K but saturates at a level that grows with N (Θ(log N) in strongly convex linear regression, a power of N under Zipf data). In LLMs, saturation points grow about linearly with log N under both constant and WSD schedules. They argue this contradicts Muennighoff et al.'s assumption of an effective epoch count uniform across dataset sizes, and that future data-reuse scaling laws must model dataset size and distribution explicitly.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes repeated-data training theoretically in linear regression and uses pretraining runs with repeated tokens in one small language model. It does not reproduce the parameter/data/compute sweeps of the cited scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported reuse behavior depends on dataset size and data spectrum. The saturation-point fit uses λ = 0.75 and differs between constant and WSD learning-rate schedules; the WSD loss curves are fitted using a parametric form.

fits_no_version.finding: In linear regression trained by SGD with an optimal constant learning rate, multi-epoch risk scales like one-pass training on KN samples when K is small. For large K it depends only on N: Θ(1/N) in the strongly convex case and N^(-(a−1)/(a−b)) under a power-law spectrum. The effective reuse rate therefore saturates at Θ(log N), Θ(N^(b/(a−b))) or Θ(log^b N), depending on the spectrum; simulations match the theory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of repeating data depends on dataset size and data spectrum: larger datasets can be repeated more epochs before returns vanish (theory in linear models).

record.problems: The LLM validation-loss curves are primarily in figures; no individual loss values or uncertainty intervals are reported. The LLM experiments use one model architecture and a limited range of dataset sizes. Saturation points depend on a selected threshold and, for WSD, on predictions from fitted curves. Theoretical results are limited to specified linear-regression settings.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results relevant to the tested repeated-data scaling findings were omitted.

untested.parts: No parameter, token or compute sweep fitting a held-out-loss power law.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.

Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not studied. For repeated data, no loss power law is fitted in N or K for the LLM; only the effective reuse rate and saturation points are reported, for a single 0.3B model.
No comparison of fitted parameter, data or compute exponents, or of compute-optimal splits, across setups. Schedule dependence is shown only for the saturation-point fit.

missing.what: Saturation epochs per dataset size read from the Fig 1 legend: 500M×4.8, 1B×5.2, 2B×5.8 epochs
Log-spectrum simulation: fitted large-K exponent 2.036 vs theory b=2 (linear-regression theory check, no version)
Learning-rate-decay theory: one-pass training loses a factor κH, multi-epoch training reaches the minimax rate, so E(∞,N) ≥ 2CκH (linear-regression theory, no version)

record.verdict_notes: The theory and simulations are stylised linear-regression results; they are linked to no version and recorded in fits_no_version. Only the LLM rows bear on V5, and they use a single 0.3B model with five fresh-data sizes and no uncertainty intervals. The WSD saturation points are extrapolated from fitted curves rather than observed. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep testing held-out language-model loss as a power law in parameter count, tokens, or compute with the other factors non-bottlenecked.
No small-run fits are used to predict loss on substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep estimates loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study examines repeated-data training, but does not establish a general held-out language-model loss power law across other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper studies reuse, dataset size, data spectrum, and learning-rate schedule, but does not compare fitted parameter/token/compute exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices.

rows.subject: strongly convex linear regression (simulation)
rows.stage_stated: SGD; learning-rate ratio grid-searched at fixed T = KN
rows.operation_detail: Synthetic experiments plot effective reuse rate against K and N.
rows.baseline: One-pass training matched at equal loss
rows.value: For log N ≪ K, E increases roughly linearly with log N; for log N ≫ K, curves flatten toward E(K,N) ≈ K
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trends; numerical point values are not stated.
rows.check: Synthetic linear-regression simulation checking the theory. Also, the row's 'log N ≪ K' and 'log N ≫ K' wording follows the paper's Sec 6.1 text, which appears to invert the theorem's regimes.

rows.stage_stated: SGD with learning rates tuned to optimal values
rows.operation_detail: Synthetic experiments plot effective reuse rate against K and log N.
rows.baseline: One-pass training matched at equal loss
rows.value: E(K,N) ≈ K for relatively small K and saturates at a value depending on N; fitted large-K exponent c2 = 0.279, reported as approximately b/(a−b) = 2/7
rows.note: The paper reports the trend and fitted exponent, without uncertainty for the fit.
rows.check: Synthetic Zipf simulation (fitted c2 = 0.279 vs theory 2/7) that verifies the theory; not a model measurement.

rows.subject: 0.3B parameter model adapted from Qwen2.5-0.5B architecture
rows.size_stated: 0.3B parameters; approximately 117 million non-embedding parameters and 331 million total parameters
rows.operation_detail: Pretraining uses fresh datasets of different sizes for up to 100 epochs; effective reuse is estimated by matching validation loss to one-pass fresh-data runs.
rows.measure: effective reuse rate E(K,N) and its saturation point
rows.baseline: One-pass run with effective fresh data size N_f(K,N), matched by validation loss
rows.value: Text reports E(K,N) ≈ K at small K (approximately ≤ 5); it increases with fresh data size and eventually saturates
rows.note: Validation-loss trajectories are shown in figures; the text reports qualitative effective-reuse results rather than individual loss values.
rows.check: The repeated-data loss matches fresh data (E≈K) only up to about 5 epochs, then saturates. The saturation epochs read from the Fig 1 legend (500M×4.8, 1B×5.2, 2B×5.8) are missing from the row.

rows.subject: 0.3B parameter model adapted from Qwen2.5-0.5B architecture
rows.operation_detail: Saturation points inferred from the validation-loss curves are fitted against fresh dataset size.
rows.measure: saturation point K(λ,N) as a function of N
rows.value: K(λ,N) ≈ 0.80 log N + 5.21; correlation coefficient r = 0.97
rows.uncertainty: Correlation coefficient r = 0.97; no interval reported
rows.note: Saturation points are estimated after EMA smoothing with decay coefficient α = 0.9 and a window size of 3 checkpoints; λ is a chosen threshold.
rows.check: This is a fit of the saturation point, not of a loss power law. It depends on the threshold λ=0.75 and on EMA smoothing, and rests on only five dataset sizes.

rows.subject: 0.3B parameter model adapted from Qwen2.5-0.5B architecture
rows.stage_stated: pretraining followed by one additional linearly decayed epoch
rows.operation_detail: Saturation points are estimated from predictions based on fitted validation-loss curves under a WSD schedule with linear decay.

conditions.value: WSD with linear decay from 10^-3 to 10^-5

rows.measure: saturation point K(λ,N) as a function of N
rows.baseline: One-pass baseline uses the same schedule as the N = 2B run
rows.value: K(λ,N) ≈ 2.35 log N + 5.25; correlation coefficient r = 0.96
rows.uncertainty: Correlation coefficient r = 0.96; no interval reported
rows.note: The loss curve form ℓ(x) = A + xBa is fitted from four selected epoch values per dataset size; the saturation points are then predicted from those fits.
rows.check: Saturation points are predicted from fitted loss curves ℓ(x)=A+B/x^a, each fitted from four checkpoints. They are not observed directly, and the log-coefficient (2.35 vs 0.80) differs from the constant-LR run.

relationships.condition: 0.3B LLM, constant LR, small number of epochs (K ≲ 5), 0.2B–2B fresh tokens
relationships.reason: In this range, repeated tokens give the same validation loss as equally many fresh tokens (E(K,N)≈K), so fresh-data scaling extends to repeated data (R15).
relationships.display_finding: Repeated tokens achieved the same validation loss as equally many fresh tokens through approximately five epochs, with effective data reuse E(K,N)≈K.

relationships.condition: 0.3B LLM, more epochs, under constant and WSD schedules
relationships.reason: Reuse benefit saturates at an epoch count that grows roughly with log N. The fitted slope differs by schedule (0.80 vs 2.35) and depends on the chosen λ threshold (R15–R17).
relationships.display_finding: The saturation epoch grew roughly logarithmically with dataset size, with fitted slopes of 0.80 and 2.35 across schedules and sensitivity to the chosen λ threshold.
